sense: a written promise to repair or replace goods

evidence: Cic. Fam. 7.18.1: Graeculam tibi mīsī cautiōnem chīrographī meī
terms.comment: In law a security or bond, written or spoken, by which one secures another against loss (Lewis & Short). Its everyday sense is care, caution: cautiō est, one must be careful (Plaut., Ter.).

evidence: Sen. Brev. Vit. 13.9: ut ad praestātiōnem scrībant (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Post-Augustan, and a jurists’ word (Lewis & Short): the being answerable for something (see guarantee, praestāre).

phrases.latin: quoniam vestrae cautiōnēs īnfirmae sunt, Graeculam tibi mīsī cautiōnem chīrographī meī
phrases.english: since you lawyers’ guarantees are worth so little, I have sent you a little Greek guarantee in my own hand

warranty.html: Lewis & Short gives cautiō as “an obligation, security, bond, warranty, bail”; its use for a maker’s or seller’s guarantee on goods is ours.

sources: Lewis & Short: cautio · Lewis & Short: praestatio
